articles.title: In 2016, Texas residents began challenging developer control of their neighbourhood associations; 10 years later, the homeowners own their park, roads, ponds and guardhouse after a long legal fight
articles.summary: For years, residents of La Bota Ranch in Laredo, Texas, questioned why developers continued to control their homeowners’ associations while residents paid
articles.body: For years, residents of La Bota Ranch in Laredo, Texas, questioned why developers continued to control their homeowners’ associations while residents paid rising fees to maintain their community. A decade after homeowners began organising against the arrangement, the associations have taken ownership of the neighbourhood’s common areas, including its park, streets, ponds and guardhouse. According to the Laredo Morning Times’ October 26, 2026, report, which quotes longtime resident and Laredo City Council member Vanessa Perez, the transfer was completed on August 20, 2026, following years of litigation and settlement negotiations. The transfer followed years of disputes over rising fees, developer control and the management of the community’s shared property.Rising fees prompted homeowners to organiseLa Bota Ranch is a master-planned residential community in north Laredo, developed in the early 1990s. Its two homeowners’ associations oversee different sections of the neighbourhood and fund services such as private road maintenance and the upkeep of parks and other facilities.The dispute gained momentum in 2016, when homeowners saw substantial increases in their association dues. According to a July 2017 report by Laredo Morning Times, annual fees for the La Bota Ranch Owners Association rose from $1,328 in 2015 to $2,268 in 2016. Fees for the La Bota Property Owners Association increased from $1,651 to $2,600 over the same period.Residents questioned the increases and raised concerns about declining services, spending and their lack of representation on the association boards. The developers continued to control the boards, while homeowners argued that they should have a greater say in decisions affecting their properties and shared amenities. In June 2017, five residents filed a lawsuit against developer Albert F. Muller III and other individuals associated with the developer-controlled boards. The case sought accountability and greater homeowner representation in the management of the associations.A jury sided with residents after years of litigationThe dispute continued for several years as homeowners challenged the developers’ control and sought changes to the associations’ governance. Residents also raised concerns about the boards’ financial decisions and their fiduciary responsibilities. In March 2022, a jury ruled in favour of the homeowners. According to KGNS and Laredo Morning Times, the jury found that the defendants had breached their fiduciary duties. The dispute involved concerns about fee increases and whether the developer-controlled boards had fulfilled their responsibilities to homeowners.In July 2022, Webb County Judge Joe Lopez ordered four board members, Albert Muller III, Albert Muller Jr., Virginia Muller and Greg Ebe, to be removed from their positions and prohibited them from directly or indirectly managing, supervising, directing or approving decisions made on behalf of either association. A new homeowner board was appointed on January 19, 2023. However, the change in board membership did not immediately resolve the dispute over control of the community’s land and common property. The associations continued working towards a settlement that would transfer ownership of the shared areas to the homeowners.Dispute over nearby development added another challengeWhile the governance dispute continued, residents also opposed a proposed warehouse near Muller Elementary School. Homeowners raised concerns about the compatibility of industrial development with the surrounding residential area. In 2024, Laredo adopted an ordinance restricting the parking or storage of certain large commercial vehicles near schools, parks and other specified locations, according to Perez’s account in the October 2026 report. The property owner subsequently challenged the city and Perez over the restriction. In November 2025, the city settled the dispute by purchasing the contested property.Separately, the associations filed another lawsuit against the developers in October 2024 involving governance, property ownership and related rights. Settlement agreements began in February 2026, initiating the transition towards homeowner control.Homeowners take ownership of shared propertyThe final transfer marked a significant change for the community. On August 20, 2026, the associations completed the closing that transferred ownership of the common-area property to the homeowners’ associations. Perez, who has lived in La Bota Ranch since 2011 and was among the residents involved in the original legal fight, described the outcome as the culmination of a decade of work by homeowners, association board members and their attorneys.The property transferred includes the community centre, park, streets, soccer field, ponds, guardhouse and other common areas. The associations’ ownership gives the homeowner-controlled bodies responsibility for these shared assets, rather than leaving them under the previous developer-controlled arrangement.For La Bota Ranch homeowners, the August 2026 transfer marked the culmination of a decade-long effort to gain greater control over their community’s governance and shared property. articles.title: Bereaved families will not face tax bill over pension delays under new rules
articles.summary: Campaigners had warned some families could face an unfair financial penalty because of delays which were not their fault.
articles.body:
Bereaved families will no longer be hit by an unexpected tax bill because of severe delays paying out civil service pensions, following a change in Wednesday's Budget.

Under previous HMRC rules, certain lump sum pension payments had to be paid within two years of the pension scheme being notified of a death to remain tax-free.

Campaigners had warned some families could face an unfair financial penalty because of delays which were not their fault.

The government has now changed the rules so payments will no longer become taxable solely because more than two years has passed.

The Civil Service Pension scheme manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK.

Outsourcing firm Capita took over the administration of the scheme from a company called MyCSP in December 2025, saying it inherited a backlog of more than 86,000 cases.

Despite a two-year transition period to prepare for the takeover, problems have persisted and by February the backlog had grown to 120,000 cases.

Retired civil servants and bereaved families have been left waiting months for pension payments, with some struggling to pay bills.

According to the latest figures up to 30 September , 1,643 outstanding cases of bereavement or death in service are more than 100 days old.

The Cabinet Office, which has overall responsibility for the Civil Service Pension Scheme, previously said only a small number of these cases were approaching the two-year threshold.

However the PCS union, which represents civil servants, had warned there were "serious questions" over how long cases would remain unresolved.

Civil service pension backlog 'overwhelmed' Capita, boss says

Emergency loans offered to civil servants waiting on pensions

Retired civil servants left in pension limbo

Rob Wassell, 58, had to wait more than two years following the death of his brother until he finally received the lump sum from his civil service pension on Tuesday.

After his case was highlighted by the BBC last week, Rob says he got a call from the pension scheme's complaints department who told him the payment was on its way.

However, because it was made after two years it was taxed at 45%, amounting to thousands of pounds.

If the payment was made after the rule change, it would not have been subject to tax.

Rob told the BBC he was pleased the government had addressed the issue in the Budget as this would mean others in his situation would not face a tax bill.

While he said he was happy to finally get his payment it was "a bitter pill to swallow" as he is now waiting for the outcome of a complaint review to find out if the tax will be reimbursed.

Rob said he was hopeful he would get the money back, adding: "I don't want to have to fight it anymore, it's been an ordeal already."

Pensions minister Torsten Bell confirmed the rule change in a letter to the chairman of Parliament's Public Accounts Committee , Conservative MP Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who had raised concerns about the issue after it was highlighted by BBC Radio 4's Money Box Live programme.

Bell said the move would "make the position fairer for all grieving families and friends where there are delays in the payment of death benefits, whether in the Civil Service or any other pensions scheme".

He added: "Removing the tax deadline does not remove [a pension scheme's] wider duties to administer schemes prudently and without avoidable delay."

Under the previous rules, if someone died before the age of 75, a pension lump sum death benefit was only tax-free if it was paid within two years of the pension scheme first becoming aware of the death, and if the value was below the deceased's Lump Sum and Death Benefit Allowance.

However, the government has now removed the two-year deadline so payments will no longer become taxable solely because they were made more than two years after a pension scheme was notified of the death.

The change applies to payments made from 28 October.

In his letter, the pensions minister said people who had already been impacted by avoidable delays and been taxed as a result could seek compensation through the pension scheme's complaints process and the Pensions Ombudsman.

Sir Geoffrey welcomed the announcement but said it does not "absolve Capita from processing and making payments to members of this scheme in a timely manner".

Fran Heathcote, general secretary of the PCS union, also welcomed the change but said "this situation should never have arisen in the first place".

She added: "Bereaved families must not pay the price for failures in the pension system.

"Capita is not off the hook, it continues to fail members and their families, which is why the scheme must be brought back in-house."

Capita has previously apologised for the impact of delays on pension scheme members and their families.

The company has said it is working to resolve outstanding cases as quickly as possible, with a particular focus on people who have been waiting the longest and those facing financial hardship or challenging circumstances.

articles.title: Oldham Coliseum's Macbeth cut short at Liquid and Envy nightclub
articles.summary: Oldham Council is seeking an explanation while ticket holders are promised automatic refunds.
articles.body:
The curtain has come down early on a production in a town's last remaining nightclub of one of Shakespeare's most famous tragedies.

The Oldham Coliseum Theatre's version of Macbeth began previews at Liquid and Envy on 23 October and had been due to run until 7 November.

The theatre apologised and said all ticket holders would automatically receive full refunds. Cast and crew members will be paid in line with their contracts.

Oldham Council said it was disappointed and would work with the Coliseum's board to understand the "unforeseen circumstances" behind the decision.

A theatre spokesperson said: "We are very sorry to have cancelled Macbeth, and we recognise the disappointment this has caused audiences and the wider Oldham community."

They said cancelling a production was never easy, particularly after the considerable work involved, and that more information would be shared as soon as possible.

A council spokesperson said it wanted ticket holders to be reimbursed promptly and for cast and crew members to receive appropriate support.

"We will be working with the Coliseum Board to better understand the unforeseen circumstances that led to this decision," they said.

Former Coronation Street star Julie Hesmondhalgh, who recently starred in the BBC's Celebrity Traitors, is also offering refunds to people who donated to her fundraising appeal to help those who could not afford tickets.

Her GoFundMe campaign raised £1,855 from 53 donations, with an earlier update saying the money would allow more than 70 people to attend the show.

Hesmondhalgh apologised and asked donors to contact her directly to arrange a full refund.

The production, directed by Nick Bagnall, was set in the 1970s, with the nightclub transformed into a world of gangsters and casinos.

Speaking before the cancellation, Bagnall said: "I want to blow the dust off Shakespeare."

The theatre said the rest of its autumn and winter programme would go ahead as planned at venues across Oldham.

The Coliseum's permanent building on Fairbottom Street is undergoing refurbishment and is expected to reopen in 2027 after an additional £7m was agreed to fund essential work.

articles.title: Worcester content creator describes life-changing impact of stroke at 22
articles.summary: Saskia Bishop says her life changed in a split second when she suffered a severe brain bleed.
articles.body:
Up until spring 2025, the life of content creator and PR executive Saskia Bishop was a glamorous whirlwind.

When she was not unboxing beauty products on social media, she could be found enjoying herself at gigs or jetting off to Paris with her friends for the city's fashion week.

That all changed on 21 April last year, when the then-22-year-old fell ill with a terrible headache after getting off a rollercoaster at a theme park in Southend, Essex.

"I just got this massive sharp bang in my head. It was like a bomb had gone off," said Saskia, who lives between Worcester and Gloucester.

"I was in so much pain that I couldn't tell my parents what was going on with me."

Saskia was having a stroke - specifically, a brain bleed caused by a ruptured arteriovenous malformation, an abnormal cluster of blood vessels connecting arteries and veins.

She lost the ability to speak, began to vomit violently and became disoriented, as her dad Scott called for an ambulance to take her to hospital.

After time in intensive care and a 7.5-hour operation, she had to spend many months recovering.

It would be a month before she could speak at all and another three before she could hold a conversation, while she also had to learn to walk again.

About 18 months later, the 23-year-old said she remembered the whole experience from the second it started.

She recalled an "extreme amount of pain" and being very confused, adding: "I didn't know what was going on and I couldn't speak. I think I was most confused about that."

Scott said he was unsure Saskia would survive and described it as the "most haunting" experience of his life.

"Some of the emotions and feelings will stay with me forever," he added, though he said he now felt a deep sense of gratitude and relief for her recovery.

Saskia barely left the house for nine months and initially struggled to come to terms with how much her life had changed.

"I was very busy all the time, being your typical 22-year-old girl, and then within a second, I was immediately isolated from normal life," she said.

"That was really difficult, to be by myself all the time."

As well as suffering with neurological fatigue, Saskia said she developed a form of obsessive compulsive disorder and became sensitive to loud noises and bright lights.

"The smallest things will immediately zap your energy," she added. "Even having conversations were completely tiring me out.

"People just don't understand it and a lot of people who have spent a lot of time with me still don't understand it."

But along with support from friends and family, she said connecting with other people who had been through similar situations helped her to get through it.

"That really changed my recovery to make me realise I'm not alone," Saskia added.

Her story will be among those told on the Channel 4 documentary Trauma: My Broken Brain, due to air at 22:00 GMT on Monday.

She said doing the show was "very cathartic" and she wanted to help other young people with similar health problems.

"Everything I do will hopefully improve the world for young stroke survivors or people who have had a massive life shift in a split second," she said.

"It leaves you in a bit of an identity crisis, you're kind of lost."

Asked if she had any advice for those going through similar experiences, she urged them to stop comparing themselves to "who they were before".

"You'll see so much more progress because you're never going to be the person you were before and that's OK," Saskia added.

"You've had a massive life-changing event and that applies to anyone else who has had a serious life trauma that changes you over night."

The NHS says the main symptoms of a stroke can happen suddenly and are remembered using the acronym FAST:

Face: One side of the face may droop and it may be difficult to smile

Arms: Weakness or numbness may make it hard to raise both arms and keep them there

Speech: Speech may become slurred or confused

Time: Call 999 immediately if you think someone is having a stroke

articles.title: Met refers itself to police watchdog over Meghan letter
articles.summary: The police force faces scrutiny over its handling of a letter containing allegations about Meghan's father.
articles.body:
The Metropolitan Police has referred itself to the police complaints watchdog over its handling of a letter with allegations against Thomas Markle, which was handed to his daughter, the Duchess of Sussex, in 2019.

The letter, written by Markle's first wife Roslyn Loveless, is believed to have contained claims about Meghan's father.

Markle has strongly denied recent allegations that he had possessed images of child abuse, describing them as "sick lies".

The force said it had voluntarily referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) "in respect of the decision not to inform other law enforcement agencies, and the decision to pass the letter to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex."

The Met added it intended to make further referrals to "relevant overseas law enforcement agencies", a process which it expected to be completed "in the coming days".

The letter that will be considered by the IOPC was sent to the Met's royal protection team by Roslyn Loveless, who divorced Thomas Markle in 1975 and died in 2024.

The handwritten letter was then passed to Meghan in January 2019, with the duchess saying last week that it had "made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father".

Meghan did not provide any details but said it had given her sufficient reason for not visiting Thomas Markle and not allowing him to meet his grandchildren, Archie and Lilibet.

Scotland Yard said the letter contained claims about offending outside the UK and that it had been forwarded to "the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness".

Confirming that it had referred itself to the IPOC, the Metropolitan Police said it was aware of media reports that it had try to obtain a copy of the letter.

"While the letter did not actually contain any information specifically related to security matters, it did contain a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom," it said.

It added that the Met has carried out an initial review in recent days which has led to the voluntary referral to IOPC.

The watchdog will consider why the Met did not share the contents of the letter with other law enforcement agencies, in the UK or overseas, it contained claims of alleged offences.

There are also reports that the Met did not keep a copy of the letter and had to get a copy from the Sussexes.

Meghan, in a statement last week, said she believed the allegations in the letter "were being investigated".

But the watchdog will have to consider what happened to the warnings.

There are also likely to be questions about what royal officials knew about the letter, which was sent when Meghan was still a working royal, and which was forwarded to the Sussexes' office rather than to her personally.

Jim Gamble, former head of the Child Exploitation and Online Protection Centre, previously told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that he would have expected the police to have shared any warnings.

"If you get information that comes to you about someone from a foreign jurisdiction who represents a threat to children, there's a well-worn path and generally you'd expect a UK police force to share that information," said Gamble.

"I would have expected the Metropolitan Police to have gone to the FBI to say, 'Look, this isn't proven, it's an allegation, you might want to look at it'.

Noel Rasmussen, Thomas Markle's granddaughter and niece of the Duchess of Sussex, told the BBC she was "deeply troubled by the questions surrounding the Metropolitan Police's handling of the information it received".

"If allegations of this seriousness were brought to the attention of authorities, it is reasonable to ask what steps were taken, why the information was not shared with other law enforcement agencies," she said.

"I believe those questions deserve clear, transparent answers."

Reports of the Met's handline of the letter emerged as Thomas Markle's son had told the police in the Philippines about material which was alleged to contain sexual images of children, which he had claimed to have found in possessions belonging to Meghan's father.

Thomas Markle had been in the Philippines in December 2025, undergoing hospital treatment, when Meghan wrote to him to end all contact.

Authorities in the Philippines have begun investigating the claims.

Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old videotapes, were handed to police by Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, last week.

However, officers in Cebu needed a court warrant before they could examine the items.

Thomas Markle Sr has strongly denied all the allegations against him. He has been backed by his daughter Samantha who has dismissed the claims against her father as "fake".

articles.title: A Connecticut couple has committed $410 million to turn a 125-acre former coal and oil power plant into a waterfront park; zoning approval moves the long-closed industrial site closer to public use
articles.summary: For decades, a stretch of Norwalk’s waterfront was defined by smokestacks, industrial machinery and the imposing presence of a coal- and oil-burning power
articles.body: For decades, a stretch of Norwalk’s waterfront was defined by smokestacks, industrial machinery and the imposing presence of a coal- and oil-burning power plant. Now, the same 125-acre peninsula overlooking Long Island Sound is poised for a radically different future. A $410 million investment from Connecticut couple Austin and Allison McChord is helping transform the former industrial site into Manresa Wilds, a public-facing destination built around open space, recreation and carefully managed cultural events.A major step for Manresa WildsAccording to the Hartford Courant and CT Mirror, Norwalk’s Planning and Zoning Commission unanimously approved a special zoning district covering the proposed Manresa Wilds development.The decision establishes the framework under which the McChords and their development team can continue refining plans for the site. The project is expected to combine parkland with amenities including walking trails, live music, private events, boat rentals and a restaurant or brewpub.The $410 million commitment includes the environmental remediation required to address the site's industrial legacy. However, the zoning decision does not represent the final approval for every element of the development. Future phases will require additional zoning reviews, detailed planning and traffic studies before construction can move forward.From industrial site to public destinationThe scale of the transformation is particularly striking because the property spent decades serving as a power-generation facility. The long-closed plant's buildings are now being incorporated into a broader vision that aims to give the waterfront a new public purpose.The first stage, known as the Northern Forest, is already under construction. As reported by the Hartford Courant and CT Mirror, the phase includes walking trails, open fields and outdoor classrooms and is expected to open next year.A later phase is expected to focus on the adaptive reuse of the former power plant's turbine hall and administration building. That portion of the project is currently targeted for completion in 2032.Community concerns reshape the plansThe redevelopment has not been without controversy. Nearby residents raised concerns about increased traffic, noise and the potential disruption caused by events at the site. More than 200 residents signed a petition opposing the proposed special zoning district and calling for a scaled-back approach.According to CT Mirror and the Hartford Courant, in response, the Manresa Wilds team conducted community meetings and collected more than 4,000 comments about the plans.Several changes followed. Plans for a hotel were removed, outdoor lighting was reduced and parking was capped at 200 spaces, with access managed through a reservation system.The approved zoning framework also places limits on events. No more than four monthly events can accommodate between 150 and 400 guests, while events drawing as many as 800 people will be restricted to four annually. On days when multiple activities take place, total attendance will be capped at 1,000.Preserving the past while opening the waterfrontThe project seeks to balance public access with the site's industrial heritage. Its redevelopment could eventually turn an inaccessible piece of Norwalk's waterfront into a destination combining nature, education, recreation and historic architecture.While concerns over traffic and neighborhood impact remain, the zoning approval marks a significant milestone. For a peninsula once associated with power generation, Manresa Wilds represents an ambitious attempt to give an industrial landscape an entirely new life—one shaped around public space and the waterfront rather than power production.Images Courtesy: Hartford Courant and istockYou use AI every day. articles.body: A 10-year-old girl who was allegedly abducted from her home in Oregon in the middle of the night was found tied up inside a closet at a house about nine miles away, nearly 13 hours later, police said.Violet Hay was taken from her family’s apartment in Canby at around 1:40 am on Wednesday after a man allegedly assaulted her 12-year-old sister with a hammer, according to local media reports. Police received a call at around 1:47 am and launched a search for the missing child.A SWAT team later found Violet at a residence in Oregon City and arrested the suspect, identified as Vince Edgar Chavez. The US Marshals Service said the girl was found tied up inside a closet. She was taken to a medical facility for treatment of injuries and further evaluation.Canby Police Chief Jose Gonzalez announced the rescue around 13 hours after the girl was reported missing.“Folks, I have great news. We found her safe and alive,” Gonzalez said, drawing applause. “As a parent, I was anxious. I’m so glad that we found her alive and well.”The police chief did not disclose whether the suspect was known to the girl’s family. An initial 911 call described the alleged abductor as an “unknown male”.Chris Owens, chief deputy district attorney for Clackamas County, described the incident as “a family’s worst nightmare”.“A young child was taken by force. Her sister was viciously assaulted,” Owens said, referring to the 12-year-old girl, who was receiving treatment at a local hospital.The suspect has not yet been formally charged. Owens said the case would be referred to the Clackamas County District Attorney’s Office to determine the charges, according to local media outlet KATU.Roommate says he had no ideaThe suspect’s roommate told KATU that he was taking a shower when police entered their Oregon City home on Wednesday afternoon. He said he had no idea that Chavez had allegedly hidden the girl inside the residence.The roommate described himself as devastated and disgusted by the incident, adding that Chavez had not displayed any concerning behaviour before the alleged kidnapping.A neighbour recorded police bringing the girl out of the house. She said she initially did not realise that the child was the same girl whose disappearance had prompted a search earlier that day.The neighbour recalled hearing a loud noise before her father told her to get down and stay away from windows and doors. She filmed the rescue from next door.After learning the identity of the child, she said she felt bad about recording the moment, adding that she felt sorry for the girl.Police investigating circumstancesPolice said the incident began when a man allegedly entered the family’s apartment at the Orchards apartment complex in Canby, assaulted the older girl and took the 10-year-old away.The older sister was taken to a hospital and was still receiving treatment on Wednesday afternoon.Investigators subsequently gathered information and reviewed surveillance footage from nearby cameras as they searched for the missing girl. Her parents cooperated with the investigation.The US Marshals Service said Chavez attempted to flee through the back of the Oregon City home as officers entered. Police arrested him without further incident.Images from the scene showed damaged windows and a garage door after officers entered the residence.Authorities have not publicly disclosed the motive behind the alleged kidnapping, how the suspect entered the family’s apartment or the full circumstances surrounding the assault.You use AI every day. articles.title: Lawyers fighting N.Y. AG’s role in Cornell assault investigation say she is not ‘viable’ as prosecutor
articles.summary: Lawyers for one of seven former Cornell fraternity members accused in a high-profile sexual assault suit argued in court that Letitia James should be removed as prosecutor.
articles.body: MONTICELLO, N.Y. — Lawyers for one of seven former Cornell University fraternity members accused in a high-profile sexual assault lawsuit argued in court Thursday that New York Attorney General Letitia James should be removed as special prosecutor, alleging she is biased against the defendants. Gillio Lopes filed a petition earlier this month seeking to block James’ appointment to oversee the case. The petition argues that James has “unequivocally demonstrated a bias and presumption of guilt against the defendants.” Lopes has denied sexually assaulting the plaintiff, who has been identified in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe. Sullivan County Supreme Court Judge James R. Farrell did not immediately rule on Lopes’ lawyers request. Lopes’ attorneys cited a social media post James published three days before she was appointed special prosecutor. “What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable,” James wrote on X on Sept. 28. “I’m holding her in my heart and in my prayers. To her, and to all survivors: you’re not alone. We stand with you.” Stuart Bernstein, one of Lopes’ attorneys, told Farrell that James had “failed” in her obligation to “represent all of the citizens of New York state.” Bernstein added that James’ appointment was no longer “viable” because her X post showed she had “publicly aligned herself” with the complainant. “She has shown that she has picked sides,” Bernstein added. James filed a formal opposition to Lopes’ efforts last week, arguing that his petition relies on claims that are “not justiciable.” She also argued that Lopes’ attorneys lack standing to challenge her appointment, which is within the governor’s discretion. Assistant Attorney General Kaitlin Vigars, speaking for James’ office, pushed back on Lopes’ lawyers contention that the X post compromised the attorney general’s ability to serve as prosecutor. “Ultimately, I don’t think public statements by a prosecutor are an impediment to a prosecution,” Vigars said in part. Lopes’ filing is known as an Article 78 petition, a proceeding that allows parties to challenge actions by state or local government officers or agencies. Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed James this month to independently investigate allegations in Jane Doe’s civil lawsuit. Doe alleges she was plied with alcohol, sexually assaulted and gang-raped at the Chi Phi fraternity house in Ithaca in October 2024. None of the seven men named in the lawsuit has been criminally charged. Hochul has defended her decision to appoint James, saying in part, “I have every confidence in our Attorney General to do what she has always done: look at the facts, examine the record and draw the proper conclusions. That’s exactly what’s going to happen in this case.” James and Hochul are both Democrats running for re-election.

articles.title: Built in 1925 and vacant for over 20 years, Texas’s historic Imperial Sugar Char House survived stalled redevelopment plans; the city has approved a $15 million rescue, with preservation work due through 2028
articles.summary: After more than two decades of vacancy, failed redevelopment plans and gradual deterioration, Sugar Land’s historic Imperial Sugar Char House is finally
articles.body: After more than two decades of vacancy, failed redevelopment plans and gradual deterioration, Sugar Land’s historic Imperial Sugar Char House is finally set to receive the rescue many residents have waited years to see. The Sugar Land City Council approved a $15 million preservation project on October 20, according to Chron, with work expected to begin later this year and finish in 2028.The Char House, built in 1925, is one of the most recognisable remnants of the Imperial Sugar refinery that helped shape the identity of Sugar Land, Texas. The building has stood empty since the refinery closed in 2003, and repeated efforts to bring the surrounding Imperial Historic District back to life never made it past the planning stage. Now the city has taken direct control of the landmark’s future and committed real money to keeping it standing.A building tied to Sugar Land’s storyThe Char House was constructed during the height of Imperial Sugar’s influence, when the refinery was not only a major employer but also the reason the community became known as Sugar Land. The building formed part of a larger industrial campus that processed and stored sugar, and its distinctive presence has long made it a symbol of the city’s origins.When the refinery portion of the campus closed in 2003, the Char House entered a long period of uncertainty. The property remained vacant for more than 20 years, and the city says the building began to deteriorate during that time. Local police also reported issues with trespassing, despite warnings, patrols and arrests around the site.For preservation supporters, the concern was never simply about saving an old industrial structure. The Char House represents a physical link to the workers, families and businesses that built Sugar Land around the sugar industry. Mayor Carol K. McCutcheon described it as more than an iconic building, calling it a connection to the community’s history and origins, as per the report.Why earlier plans failedThe site’s troubles were not caused by a lack of interest. Developers repeatedly proposed ways to redevelop the Imperial Historic District, but financing and market conditions repeatedly got in the way. The most ambitious plan arrived in 2023, when PUMA Development announced a $1 billion mixed-use redevelopment for the 20-acre district, it was reported.That proposal promised a dramatic transformation, with residential units, retail space, offices and restaurants planned across the historic site. It appeared to offer the kind of large-scale investment that could have revived the Char House and the land around it. But the developer ultimately abandoned the project after failing to secure financing, leaving the historic building in the same vulnerable condition it had occupied for years.The pattern illustrates a familiar challenge in historic preservation. Old industrial buildings can be expensive to repair, difficult to adapt and complicated to insure. Developers may see their potential, but banks and investors can hesitate when the cost of stabilising a century-old structure competes with newer construction elsewhere.In Sugar Land’s case, the city eventually decided that waiting for another private redevelopment plan carried too much risk. Officials acquired the larger Imperial Historic District in June 2025, giving the municipality control over the property and allowing it to begin addressing the building’s condition directly.What the $15 million project includesThe approved project is not a full commercial redevelopment, at least not yet. Instead, it focuses on stabilising and protecting the Char House so that it can survive long enough for a future use to be developed. The city says the work will prepare the building for eventual redevelopment and adaptive reuse.The preservation plan includes a new permanent roof, structural repairs to the exterior walls and rear liquor gallery, selective steel and masonry repairs, mechanical and electrical improvements, and restoration of the building’s windows. The city’s iconic Imperial signage will also be restored and returned to its historic location on the building.Those repairs matter because water intrusion, weakened walls and failing mechanical systems can quickly turn a vacant historic building into a safety hazard. A new roof and structural work can prevent further decay, while restored windows and improved electrical systems make future occupation more realistic. The city also says the work is designed to keep the building eligible for future historic tax credits, which could make redevelopment more financially viable later.A groundbreaking is expected on November 5, with construction mobilisation planned for December. The city estimates that the preservation work will be completed by March 2028.What could happen nextThe city has not yet announced a final tenant or a complete redevelopment plan for the restored building. However, officials say the Char House could eventually accommodate office, commercial, retail or restaurant uses as broader plans for the Imperial Historic District move forward.That flexibility is important. A restored industrial building can serve many purposes, from a restaurant or event space to offices or small commercial units. The key is that the city is first protecting the structure rather than allowing it to deteriorate further while developers wait for the right economic conditions.For residents, the project represents a shift from uncertainty to action. After years of watching proposals appear and disappear, they will soon see crews on site, scaffolding around the building and visible progress toward saving a landmark that has defined Sugar Land for a century.A second chance for a landmarkThe Char House has survived longer than many expected. It outlasted the closure of the refinery, more than 20 years of vacancy and the collapse of a billion-dollar redevelopment proposal. Now, with $15 million approved and construction scheduled through 2028, it may finally receive the care needed to become part of Sugar Land’s future as well as its past.The project will not solve every question about the wider Imperial Historic District, and the city will still need to determine how best to use the restored space. But for now, the focus is on preservation. Sugar Land is investing in the idea that some buildings are worth saving, not only because of what they once were, but because of what they can still become.You use AI every day. articles.title: Hasan Piker sues Scott Jennings for $72.5 million over ‘lynching’ claims, alleges edited clips damaged his reputation
articles.summary: Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, widely known as HasanAbi, has filed a $72.5 million defamation lawsuit against political commentator Scott Jennings.
articles.body: Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, widely known as HasanAbi, has filed a $72.5 million defamation lawsuit against political commentator Scott Jennings. The lawsuit accuses Jennings of falsely claiming that Piker supported bringing back lynchings against Black Americans. Filed on October 27, 2026, in a federal court in Washington, D.C., the case seeks $27.5 million in compensation and $45 million in punitive damages. Piker discussed the case during a livestream the same day, saying Jennings had “certainly messed up” and arguing that media commentators should be more careful about what they say publicly.Why Hasan Piker Is Seeking $72.5 Million From Scott Jennings Over the August 11, 2026, RemarksThe dispute began on August 11, when Jennings discussed Piker on The Scott Jennings Show. According to the lawsuit, Jennings told his audience that Piker was “out there calling for Black voters to be lynched” and claimed he had a “plan of returning our country to lynchings.”Jennings also shared a video on X, formerly known as Twitter, featuring clips from Piker's old Twitch livestreams. While discussing Democratic politician Abdul El-Sayed, Jennings said:“On top of these candidates, in their own words, their surrogates are just as bad. Even worse, actually. We continue today our exploration of the radical socialist streamer, Hasan Piker. Now, he's Abdul El-Sayed's best friend, and he campaigns for him all the time. And African-Americans out there, within the sound of my voice, need to listen up, and you must listen carefully. This is who socialists like Abdul El-Sayed choose to keep for company.”Piker's lawsuit argues that the video was edited to make his comments appear to support racial violence. According to the complaint, the original footage came from three separate livestreams in October 2024. His legal team says the clips were cut and rearranged, removing the context needed to understand what he was saying.The complaint also accuses Jennings of presenting words Piker never said as a direct quote. Piker argues that the video and the statements made about it gave viewers a false impression of his views.According to the lawsuit, the claims harmed his reputation and affected his work. Piker says he suffered public humiliation, emotional distress and damage to his professional interests. articles.title: Prosecutors ask judge to reject Lindsay Clancy defense’s motion to dismiss charges
articles.summary: Prosecutors have asked a judge to reject Lindsey Clancy’s motion to dismiss the charges against her, arguing in a motion that they have the right to seek justice on behalf of her three young children even after a mistrial was declared.
articles.body: Prosecutors have asked a judge to reject Lindsey Clancy’s motion to dismiss the charges against her, arguing in a motion that they have the right to seek justice on behalf of her three young children even after a mistrial was declared. “Because a mistrial was properly declared due to the manifest necessity of a deadlocked jury, the defendant’s motion to dismiss should be denied, and the Commonwealth should be permitted to continue to pursue justice for Cora, Dawson and Callan Clancy,” prosecutors wrote in the motion filed Monday. Clancy was indicted on three counts of murder and strangulation in the 2023 deaths of her three young children and her trial took place in a Massachusetts courtroom over the summer. A mistrial was declared in September when the jury told the judge it was deadlocked after seven days of deliberation — with one juror as the holdout. Clancy is accused of strangling her three children, Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and 8-month-old Callan in their Duxbury home. Her lawyers argued that she suffered from postpartum psychosis and was not criminally responsible for her actions. Her defense team moved to dismiss the charges against Clancy on the grounds of double jeopardy — a law that prevents defendants from being prosecuted more than once for the same crime. Prosecutors say the standard does not apply in the Clancy case because a verdict was not reached. The remedy to the jurors’ stalemate should not be to dismiss the charges against Clancy, but to hold a new trial, according to the prosecution’s motion. The escalating legal battle centers on the holdout juror, who said he’s been harassed since the trial ended but continues to stand by his position that Clancy premeditated the murders of her children. The other 11 jurors were prepared to acquit Clancy by the insanity standard, they have said. They have claimed the holdout juror failed to follow the standard of reasonable doubt throughout deliberations. Clancy’s attorney, Kevin Reddington, argued throughout the trial that she was in the throes of postpartum psychosis at the time of the killings and was therefore unaware of her actions and unable to control herself. The prosecution, however, argued that Clancy was not in psychosis when she killed her children, and that she planned the strangulations ahead of time. In his response Wednesday to the prosecution’s opposition to dismiss charges against Clancy, Reddington argued that a new trial without the investigation of jury misconduct would subject his client to “successive prosecution with all of the concomitant burdens and dangers that the Supreme Judicial Court has repeatedly warned against.” “This is not the law,” Reddington’s motion reads. “To the contrary, it flies in the face of centuries of Double Jeopardy jurisprudence.”

articles.title: If you hire H-1B, you won't get grants: Texas Agriculture Department's new rule for businesses; 'Taxpayers work hard for their money'
articles.summary: Texas Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller has announced that businesses employing H-1B visa holders will no longer be eligible for certain grants
articles.body: Texas Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller has announced that businesses employing H-1B visa holders will no longer be eligible for certain grants administered by the Texas Department of Agriculture, in a move aimed at prioritising local workers in the use of taxpayer money. Miller announced the policy on October 28, saying public funds should support businesses that create opportunities for Texans rather than companies that rely on temporary foreign workers.“Texas taxpayers work hard for their money. They deserve to know that their tax dollars are being used to create opportunities for Texans -- not to subsidize businesses that choose foreign labor while Texans are ready and willing to work,” Miller said.The commissioner also challenged Governor Greg Abbott and other statewide elected officials to introduce similar restrictions across their agencies, grant programmes and economic development initiatives.“Governor Abbott has publicly declared that taxpayer-funded employment should prioritize Texans. I agree -- and now it’s time to turn that principle into action,” Miller said.He urged state leaders to review existing grant and economic incentive programmes, increase transparency about recipients and ensure public funding creates opportunities for Texas workers.Which grants will be affected?The restrictions apply to eligible grants administered directly by the Texas Department of Agriculture. They do not extend to TDA-administered programs operated on behalf of independent boards, commissions or other entities that establish their own eligibility criteria.The policy also does not prevent public or private Texas entities from receiving federal grants or participating in state-funded loan programmes administered by the department.Miller said the move was intended to ensure that taxpayer-funded assistance supports Texas communities and businesses that invest in the local workforce.The announcement follows Abbott’s January 2026 directive ordering Texas state agencies and public universities to freeze new H-1B visa petitions, subject to exceptions. That directive was intended to give the state time to review its use of the visa programme and introduce safeguards to prioritise Texas workers.Miller urged other state officials to follow the agriculture department’s approach and extend similar restrictions to other publicly funded programmes.You use AI every day. articles.title: Paris suburb shooting suspect targeted people of Muslim or African appearance, prosecutor says
articles.summary: Kevin T has been charged with murder and attempted murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise.
articles.body:
A man suspected of a deadly shooting near Paris last week has admitted targeting people of "Muslim, African or North African" appearance, prosecutors say.

A man was killed and seven people including a child were injured last Friday when an attacker opened fire as he drove through two western suburbs.

On Thursday the suspect was charged with murder and attempted murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise, the national anti-terrorism prosecutor's office (PNAT) said.

President Emmanuel Macron called it a "racist terrorist attack" and anti-racism demonstrations have been held around France.

Pengo Bossio Wangi, a 26-year-old French-Congolese martial artist, was killed in the shooting.

Three of those wounded were still in hospital with one in critical condition, terrorism prosecutor Olivier Christen told reporters.

The suspect, named in French media as 39-year-old Kevin T, chose Trappes and nearby La Verrière because he saw them as a "hotbed for Islamists", he said.

Kevin T had denied any "terrorist intent", insisted his actions were "legitimate" and said he "feels no regret", Christen said.

Police found "weapons or weapon components" in the suspect's home as well as books including a Quran, a Bible and Adolf Hitler's Mein Kampf and stickers celebrating the hard-right National Rally (RN) party, Christen said.

Kevin T told investigators that he had designed the stickers with slogans such as "long live France, RN, proud to be French" himself and had them printed more than a year ago, Christen said.

But the suspect also told investigators he was not a member or supporter of any political party.

On Wednesday Macron said that "certain political movements on the far right" including the RN and "those close to them" had allowed a climate of racism "to take root".

Jean-Philippe Tanguy, a prominent RN lawmaker, retorted that it was the president himself who had allowed "hateful ideologies" to flourish.

France's presidential elections is six months away and RN leader Marine Le Pen is currently leading opinion polls.

articles.body: Jaipur: A minor collision between two motorcycles escalated into a late-night confrontation in Hasanpura Thursday where a group of people blocked Hatwara Road after one of the riders was allegedly slapped during an argument. The blockade disrupted movement on the road and heightened tension in the locality.Personnel from Sodala and Sadar police stations reached the spot after receiving information about the dispute. articles.title: Coaching body seeks probe into sealing drive
articles.summary: All Coaching Institute Mahasangh demands probe into JDA’s Jaipur sealing drive, alleging small coaching centres are targeted while larger ones stay open.
articles.body: Jaipur: All Coaching Institute Mahasangh has sought an inquiry into the Jaipur Development Authority’s (JDA) sealing drive in Gopalpura Bypass, alleging that coaching centres with fewer than 100 students were being targeted while larger institutes continue to operate.The federation alleged that provisions of the Rajasthan Coaching Centres (Control and Regulation) Act, 2025 were being misinterpreted. It maintained that establishments with fewer than 100 students fall outside the definition of coaching centres under the Act and can operate as tuition centres, including in residential premises.“JDA action should not be selective. Several small institutes, including Pathshala and Mishti Classes, have been sealed, while only basements of larger coaching institutes have been closed. This is unfair,” said Anish Kumar Nadar, state president of the federation.He said students enrolled in smaller institutes largely came from economically vulnerable backgrounds. Coaching’s closure could force students to return home as they cannot afford fees charged by larger institutes.Deputy inspector general of JDA Vigilance Wing, Anand Sharma, said the action was being carried out in compliance with Supreme Court directions. “We have not received any specific complaint in this regard so far. articles.title: Cops drag & detain protesters as teacher recruitment stir turns tense
articles.summary: Bhopal teacher recruitment protest turns tense as police detain Grade-3 candidates blocking roads for appointment letters; police deny excess, case likely.
articles.body: Bhopal: A tense confrontation broke out between police and selected (grade-3) teacher candidates here on Thursday after the aspirants blocked roads at Board Office Square, demanding immediate appointment letters and the start of the joining process.Police later detained several protesters to clear the road, triggering allegations of rough treatment that officers have rejected.The candidates have been holding a sit-in at the busy square since October 5. Frustrated by the continued delay, they moved onto the road on Thursday afternoon, sat across both sides and raised slogans, severely disrupting traffic in the area.Some protesters also banged steel plates and lay on the road as police attempted to remove them.After the removal operation, the candidates alleged that police personnel assaulted them and dragged women protesters while clearing the blockade.Police denied the charges, saying the protesters had no permission to obstruct a public road and that police acted to restore traffic movement.The police maintained that the action was limited to clearing the road and taking the demonstrators into custody. Several aspirants reportedly began singing the national anthem as they were detained. Police Commissioner Sanjay Kumar said, “The police did not engage in any form of excess. The protesters had blocked the road, causing inconvenience to the general public; therefore, they were merely taken into custody. They were released after signing a personal bond. A case will be registered against them for intentionally blocking the road.”The protesters, who are merit-listed candidates for the Primary Teacher grade-3 recruitment, say they have repeatedly sought meetings with officials but the appointment process has not progressed despite their 26-day agitation. They are demanding the immediate release of appointment letters and joining dates.According to the candidates, School Education Minister Rao Uday Pratap Singh had earlier assured them that appointments would be issued by October 16. With that deadline passing without action, they said they were left with no option but to intensify their protest by blocking the road.The incident has intensified attention on the prolonged impasse between the selected candidates and the School Education Department. The aspirants remain firm that they will continue their agitation until the government begins the appointment process, while police have indicated that any further attempt to block the road without permission may invite action.Officials had not announced a fresh timeline for issuing the appointment letters till the time of reporting.
